claim: Two monkeys were trained to perform a Cue-Set-Go (CSG) motor timing task in which they had to produce either an 800 ms (Short) or a 1500 ms (Long) time interval either with a saccade (Eye) or with a button press (Hand).
source: Two monkeys were trained to perform a Cue-Set-Go (CSG) motor timing task (Figure 1A). On each trial, animals had to produce either an 800 ms (Short) or a 1500 ms (Long) time interval (tt) either with a saccade (Eye) or with a button press (Hand).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental task design used in the study.

claim: The task consisted of four randomly interleaved trial types: Eye-Short (ES), Eye-Long (EL), Hand-Short (HS), and Hand-Long (HL).
source: The task thus consisted of four randomly interleaved trial types, Eye-Short (ES), Eye-Long (EL), Hand-Short (HS), and Hand-Long (HL).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the trial types in the experimental design.

claim: Animals learned to use the Cue and flexibly switched between the four trial types on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: Animals learned to use the Cue and flexibly switched between the four trial types on a trial-by-trial basis (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral performance data showing successful task execution.

claim: There were no errors associated with using the wrong effector.
source: There were no errors associated with using the wrong effector, and the number of errors with respect to the target interval was extremely small (~0.79% misclassified trials based on fits to a Gaussian mixture model).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of behavioral errors.

claim: Produced intervals (tp) were more variable for the Long compared to the Short interval for both effectors.
source: For both effectors, a robust feature of the behavior was that produced intervals (tp) were more variable for the Long compared to the Short (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of behavioral variability across conditions.

claim: Timing variability scales with the interval being timed, consistent with scalar variability.
source: This is consistent with the common observation that timing variability scales with the interval being timed (Gibbon, 1977; Malapani and Fairhurst, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature to support the observed pattern.

claim: The scalar variability was evident in the linear relationship between mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of tp in each behavioral session.
source: This scalar variability was evident in the linear relationship between mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of tp in each behavioral session (Figure 1C, the slope of the linear test was significantly positive, one-tailed t-test, p<<0.001, for monkey A, df = 128, t = 32.12; for monkey D, p<<0.001, df = 163, t = 24.06).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical tests confirming the linear relationship.

claim: tp exhibited significant serial correlations up to a trial lag of 20 or more in all four trial types.
source: In all four trial types, tp exhibited significant serial correlations up to a trial lag of 20 or more (p<0.01, dash lines: 1% and 99% confidence bounds by estimating the null distribution from shuffled series, Figure 2A) revealing strong slowly fluctuating sources of variability.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of serial correlations with significance testing.

claim: Serial correlations were stronger between trials with the same effector and same target interval compared to trials that were associated with different target intervals and/or different effectors.
source: Importantly, these correlations were stronger between trials with the same effector and same tt compared to trials that were associated with different tt and/or different effectors (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative analysis of correlations across different trial type transitions.

claim: The context-specificity of serial correlations suggests that they were not solely due to non-specific fluctuations of internal states such as the overall level of alertness.
source: The context-specificity of these correlations suggests that they were not solely due to non-specific fluctuations of internal states such as the overall level of alertness, which should persist across the four randomly interleaved trial types.
evidence: The manuscript provides logical inference based on the context-specificity of the observed correlations.

claim: The slow fluctuations of tp in the CSG task were a signature of drift in memory.
source: As expected, tp serial correlations diminished significantly in the control task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; p<<0.001, paired sample t-test, t19 = 4.9, on the partial correlation between CSG and controls, trial lag was limited to 20 trials), suggesting that the slow fluctuations of tp in the CSG task were a signature of drift in memory.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from a control experiment designed to test the memory drift hypothesis.

claim: μ(en) increased monotonically with en-1.
source: Results revealed that these error statistics were highly structured across trials: μ(en) increased monotonically with en-1, and σ(en) had a U-shaped profile (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of error statistics across consecutive trials.

claim: σ(en) had a U-shaped profile with respect to en-1.
source: Results revealed that these error statistics were highly structured across trials: μ(en) increased monotonically with en-1, and σ(en) had a U-shaped profile (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of error statistics across consecutive trials.

claim: The U-shaped relationship between σ(en) and en-1 suggests that animals increase their behavioral variability when the reward is low and decrease it when the reward is high.
source: In contrast, the U-shaped relationship between σ(en) and en-1 is unexpected and suggests that trial outcome regulates behavior variability. In particular, since smaller errors were associated with higher average rewards, this U-shaped relationship suggests that animals increase their behavioral variability when the reward is low and decrease it when the reward is high.
evidence: The manuscript provides interpretation of the observed U-shaped relationship in terms of reward-dependent variability regulation.

claim: σ(en) was significantly correlated with the magnitude of the previous reward rn-1.
source: A more refined binning of trials based on the magnitude of reward provided evidence that the effect was graded: σ(en) was significantly correlated with the magnitude of the previous reward rn-1 (Spearman's correlation, ρ = −0.23, ***p=2e-15, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical correlation analysis between variability and reward magnitude.

claim: The effect of reward on variability was progressively weaker for larger trial lags.
source: Finally, the effect of reward was progressively weaker for larger trial lags (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E) revealing the lingering effects of reward (or lack thereof) beyond single trials.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of reward effects across different trial lags.

claim: The modulation of variability was most strongly and consistently present across trials of the same type.
source: Results indicated that (1) correlations were strongest between pairs of trials of the same type as expected from our previous cross-correlation analysis in (Figure 2B) and (2) the modulation of variability was most strongly and consistently present across trials of the same type.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis comparing variability modulation across same versus different trial types.

claim: Human behavior exhibited long-term serial correlations and these correlations were context (effector) specific.
source: Similar to monkeys, human behavior exhibited long-term serial correlations and these correlations were context (effector) specific (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of human behavioral data showing similar patterns to monkeys.

claim: In humans, μ(en) increased monotonically with en-1 and σ(en) had a U-shaped profile with respect to en-1.
source: Results were qualitatively similar: μ(en) increased monotonically with en-1 verifying the presence of slow drifts, and σ(en) had a U-shaped with respect to en-1 indicating that subjects used the feedback to regulate their variability (Figure 3C and Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of human error statistics showing similar patterns to monkeys.

claim: In humans, the effect of reward on variability was context-specific.
source: Finally, similar to monkeys, the effect of reward on variability was context-specific (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of context-specificity in human data.

claim: The presence or absence of reward had a causal impact on behavioral variability that was not mediated through the size of error.
source: Across subjects and irrespective of the size of error, variability was significantly larger after incorrect compared to correct trials (Figure 4D). In other words, the presence or absence of reward had a causal impact on behavioral variability that was not mediated through the size of error.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from a probabilistic reward experiment designed to test causality.

claim: The RSGP model was able to capture both the long-term effect of memory drift and the short-term effect of reward on variability.
source: RSGP was able to capture both the long-term effect of memory drift, and the short-term effect of reward on variability.
evidence: The manuscript reports model fitting results showing the RSGP captures key behavioral features.

claim: The recovered characteristic length associated with serial correlations (lSE) were invariably larger than that of the reward-dependent kernel (lRS).
source: The recovered characteristic length associated with serial correlations (lSE) were invariably larger than that of the reward-dependent kernel (lRS) (Monkeys: lSE = 20.6 ± 21.4, lRS = 2.0 ± 0.7; Humans: lSE = 19.2 ± 21.8, lRS = 1.3 ± 0.4; Median ±MAD).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative model parameters from fits to behavioral data.

claim: The RSGP model was able to accurately capture the relationship of μ(en) and σ(en) to en-1.
source: Importantly, across both monkeys and humans, the model was able to accurately capture the relationship of μ(en) and σ(en) to en-1 (Figure 5C, and Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports model validation results comparing model predictions to behavioral data.

claim: The RSGP model was able to capture the modulation of behavioral variability in the probabilistic reward experiment.
source: Second, the RSGP was also able to capture the modulation of behavioral variability in the probabilistic reward experiment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports model validation on independent experimental data.

claim: The RL-based MCMC sampling model could not capture the U-shaped relationship between σ(en) and en-1.
source: However, when the model was parameterized to capture the monotonic relationship between μ(en) and en-1, it could not capture the U-shaped relationship between σ(en) and en-1 (s2 = 0.045 [-0.048 0.14], Figure 6C, middle).
evidence: The manuscript reports model comparison results showing limitations of alternative models.

claim: The DS model exhibited unstable 'run-away' behavior where it could easily lose track of the target interval.
source: However, upon close examination, we found the behavior of the DS model to be unstable. Specifically, unlike the MCMC and RSGP models (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C), the DS model could easily lose track of the target interval and exhibit 'run-away' behavior, that is, generate tp values that deviated from tt for an extended number of consecutive trials (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports simulation results showing instability of the DS model.

claim: The probability of run-away behavior in the DS model in a typical 2000 trial session was 65.1 ± 1.2%.
source: Simulating the model with the parameters fit to animals' behavior, the probability of run-away behavior in a typical 2000 trial session was 65.1 ± 1.2% (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative simulation results for the DS model.

claim: The DS model was unable to capture the U-shaped relationship between σ(en) and en-1 even for the subset of simulations without run-away behavior.
source: For this subset of DS simulations, the model was able to capture the dependencies between consecutive trials relating μ(en) to en-1 (Figure 6D; m1 = 0.46 [0.44 0.48]), but not the U-shaped relationship between σ(en) and en-1 (Figure 6D; s2 = −0.046 [−0.061 −0.03]).
evidence: The manuscript reports model comparison results for the DS model.

claim: Both the MCMC and DS models were unable to capture the long-term correlations that were present in the behavioral data and the simulations of the RSGP model.
source: We also note that both the MCMC and DS models were unable to capture the long-term correlations that were present in the behavioral data and the simulations of the RSGP model (Figure 6, bottom).
evidence: The manuscript reports model comparison results showing limitations of alternative models.

claim: The monotonic relationship between μ(en) and en-1 was stronger after trials that subjects received positive feedback.
source: The monotonic relationship between μ(en) and en-1 was stronger after trials that subjects received positive feedback (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and this effect was consistent with the behavior of the RSGP model (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of human data from the probabilistic reward experiment.

claim: Population activity in the thalamus, DMFC, and caudate exhibited slow fluctuations in register with memory drifts.
source: We found strong evidence that neural activity in all three areas exhibited slow fluctuations in register with memory drifts. In 91%, ~79%, and ~45% of sessions, the activity along the drift direction in the thalamus (zTh), DMFC (zDMFC), and caudate (zCd), respectively, was significantly correlated with eslow (Figure 7B–D, p<0.01, null hypothesis test by shuffling trials).
evidence: The manuscript reports neural data analysis showing correlations between neural activity and behavioral drifts.

claim: In the thalamus, μ(zn) had a monotonic relationship with en-1 for trials of the same type.
source: Results were consistent with this prediction as evidenced by the slope of a linear regression model relating μ(zn) to en-1 (filled circles in Figure 8B–D top, Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports neural data analysis showing relationships between neural activity and behavioral errors.

claim: The monotonic relationship between μ(zn) and en-1 was absent for consecutive trials associated with different effectors.
source: Moreover, this relationship was absent for consecutive trials associated with different effectors (open circles in Figure 8B–D top, Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports neural data analysis showing context-specificity of neural-behavioral relationships.

claim: In the thalamus, σ(znTh) exhibited a U-shaped profile with respect to en-1.
source: In thalamus, σ(znTh) exhibited the characteristic U-shape profile with respect to en-1 (Figure 8B bottom), which we verified quantitatively by comparing the variance of znTh for rewarded and unrewarded trials (p<0.01, two-sample F-test for equal variances on znTh, F(5608,4266) = 1.08 for negative en-1 and p<0.001 for positive en-1, F(4723,6125) = 1.28), and by testing the profile using quadratic regression (see Materials and methods; Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of thalamic neural variability.

claim: In the thalamus, there was no significant relationship between σ(znTh) and en-1 for consecutive trials associated with different effectors.
source: As an important control, we performed the same analysis between consecutive trials associated with different effectors and we found no significant relationship between σ(znTh) and en-1 (p=0.91, two-sample F-test for equal variances, F(5332,3984) = 1.0 for the negative en-1; p=0.97 for the positive en-1, F(4234,5857) = 0.99).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing context-specificity of thalamic variability modulation.

claim: In DMFC and caudate, variability along the memory drift was relatively independent of en-1.
source: Unlike the thalamus, in DMFC and caudate, variability along the memory drift was relatively independent of en-1 (Figure 8C bottom, 8D bottom), that is, σ(znDMFC) and σ(znCd) were not significantly different after rewarded and unrewarded trials (two-sample F-test for equal variances, F(6244,4818) = 0.87, p=0.99 for the negative en-1; F(4825,7572) = 1.002, p=0.021 for the positive en-1, see Figure 8—figure supplement 1 for each animal separately).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing lack of reward-dependent variability modulation in DMFC and caudate.

claim: The effect of reward in DMFC and caudate was not aligned to the drift direction (β) associated with the slow fluctuations.
source: Together, these results provide evidence that the effect of reward in DMFC and caudate was not aligned to the β associated with the slow fluctuations.
evidence: The manuscript provides interpretation of neural data analysis results.

claim: An unconstrained decoding strategy aimed at simultaneously capturing both components of errors could find directions along which the slow fluctuations and the effect of reward are aligned in all three areas.
source: We note, however, that an unconstrained decoding strategy aimed at simultaneously capturing both components of errors could find directions along which the slow fluctuations and the effect of reward are aligned in all three areas (Figure 8—figure supplement 3, Table 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from an alternative neural data analysis approach.

claim: Learning reduces variability but variability can facilitate learning.
source: Learning reduces variability but variability can facilitate learning.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle motivating the study.

claim: Two opposing factors contribute to timing variability: slow memory fluctuation that degrades performance and reward-dependent exploratory behavior that improves performance.
source: We identified two opposing factors contributing to timing variability: slow memory fluctuation that degrades performance and reward-dependent exploratory behavior that improves performance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Signatures of memory drift and reward-dependent exploration were evident across populations of neurons in DMFC, DMFC-projecting neurons in the ventrolateral thalamus, and putative target of DMFC in the caudate.
source: Signatures of these opposing factors were evident across populations of neurons in the dorsomedial frontal cortex (DMFC), DMFC-projecting neurons in the ventrolateral thalamus, and putative target of DMFC in the caudate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Only in the thalamus were the performance-optimizing regulation of variability aligned to the slow performance-degrading memory fluctuations.
source: However, only in the thalamus were the performance-optimizing regulation of variability aligned to the slow performance-degrading memory fluctuations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Variability caused by exploratory behavior might help to mitigate other undesirable sources of variability.
source: These findings reveal how variability caused by exploratory behavior might help to mitigate other undesirable sources of variability and highlight a potential role for thalamocortical projections in this process.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Thalamocortical projections may play a role in using exploratory behavior to mitigate undesirable sources of variability.
source: These findings reveal how variability caused by exploratory behavior might help to mitigate other undesirable sources of variability and highlight a potential role for thalamocortical projections in this process.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Reinforcement learning has been extremely valuable in explaining behavior when an agent has to choose among a small number of discrete options.
source: RL has been extremely valuable in explaining behavior when an agent has to choose among a small number of discrete options, such as classic multi-armed bandit problems (Daw et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature to establish the context for the study.

claim: Learning through trial and error is critical when the action space is large and continuous.
source: However, learning through trial and error is also critical when the action space is large and continuous (Dhawale et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature to establish the context for the study.

claim: Classic RL is not feasible when the action space is continuous because it requires the agent to compute the value function over an infinitude of parameters.
source: In this case, classic RL is not feasible as it requires the agent to compute the value function over an infinitude of parameters (e.g. all the kinematic variables associated with a reach and grasp movement).
evidence: The manuscript provides logical reasoning about limitations of classic RL.

claim: One hypothesis is that the brain directly regulates variability to facilitate learning in continuous action spaces.
source: One intriguing hypothesis is that the brain directly regulates variability to facilitate learning (Kao et al., 2005; Ölveczky et al., 2005; Tumer and Brainard, 2007; Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature proposing this hypothesis.

claim: The basic idea of variability regulation is that the agent reduces variability when a trial yields reward and increases variability in the absence of reward.
source: The basic idea is that the agent reduces variability when a trial yields reward (i.e. exploit previously rewarded action) and increases variability in the absence of reward (i.e. explore new possibilities).
evidence: The manuscript describes the theoretical framework for variability regulation.

claim: Humans learn more efficiently if the structure of their natural movement variability aligns with the underlying learning objective.
source: For example, humans learn more efficiently if the structure of their natural movement variability aligns with the underlying learning objective (Wu et al., 2014), reaching movements become more variable during periods of low success rate (Izawa and Shadmehr, 2011; Pekny et al., 2015), and saccades become more variable in the absence of reward (Takikawa et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature providing evidence for variability regulation.

claim: One of the primary functions of motor learning is to reduce variability.
source: Although increasing motor variability may play a direct role in the induction of learning (Dhawale et al., 2017), one of the primary functions of motor learning is to reduce variability (Crossman, 1959; Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Thoroughman and Shadmehr, 2000; Smith et al., 2006; Sternad and Abe, 2010; Verstynen and Sabes, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature establishing the dual role of variability in learning.

claim: A circuit comprised of DMFC, DMFC-projecting thalamus and caudate plays a causal role in the control of movement initiation time.
source: Recently, we identified a cortico-basal ganglia circuit that plays a causal role in animals' performance during a flexible timing behavior (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work by the authors establishing the role of this circuit.

claim: Animals control movement initiation time by adjusting a tonic signal in the thalamus that sets the speed at which activity in DMFC and caudate evolve toward an action-triggering state.
source: A combination of population data analysis and modeling revealed that animals control the movement initiation time by adjusting a tonic signal in the thalamus that sets the speed at which activity in the dorsomedial frontal cortex (DMFC) and caudate evolve toward an action-triggering state.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work by the authors describing the mechanism of timing control.

claim: Reward was provided when the relative error was within an experimentally-controlled acceptance window.
source: Reward was provided when the relative error, defined as e = (tp-tt)/tt (Figure 1A) was within an experimentally-controlled acceptance window.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental reward contingency.

claim: On rewarded trials, the magnitude of reward decreased linearly with the size of the error.
source: On rewarded trials, the magnitude of reward decreased linearly with the size of the error.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental reward structure.

claim: The width of the acceptance window was controlled independently for each trial type using a one-up-one-down staircase procedure.
source: The width of the acceptance window was controlled independently for each trial type using a one-up-one-down staircase procedure (see Materials and methods) so that animals received reward on nearly half of the trials (Figure 1C, inset).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure for controlling reward rate.

claim: Hand trials were more variable than Eye trials.
source: Hand trials were more variable than Eye ones (one-tailed paired-sample t-test, for monkey A, n = 95, t52 = 6.92, ***p<<0.001, and for monkey D, n = 108, t61 = 6.51, ***p<<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of variability between effectors.

claim: In both animals, the variability was significantly larger for the Long compared to the Short for both effectors.
source: In both animals, the variability was significantly larger for the Long compared to the Short for both effectors (one-tailed paired-sample t test, ***p<<0.001, for monkey A, n = 190, t128 = 157.4; for monkey D, n = 216, t163 = 181.7).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of variability between intervals.

claim: Regression slopes relating σ(tp) to μ(tp) were positive and significantly different from zero for both effectors.
source: Regression slopes were positive and significantly different from zero for both effectors (β = 0.087 ± 0.02 mean±std for Eye and 0.096 ± 0.021 for Hand in Monkey A; β1 = 0.10 ± 0.02 for Eye and 0.12 ± 0.021 for Hand in Monkey D).
evidence: The manuscript reports regression analysis results showing scalar variability.

claim: Serial correlations were stronger between trials with the same effector and same interval compared to trials with the same effector but different interval.
source: Serial correlations were stronger between trials with the same effector and interval compared to trials with the same effector but different interval (*** dark gray, paired sample t-test on two sets of cross-correlations with less than 20 trial lags and combining four trial types; monkey A: p<<0.001, n = 80, t79 = 9.8; monkey D: p<<0.001, n = 80, t79 = 5.8), and trials of the different effector but same interval (*** light gray, monkey A: p<<0.001, n = 80, t79 = 6.7; monkey D: p<<0.001, n = 80, t79 = 17.3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of serial correlations across different trial type transitions.

claim: In the same effector condition, variability increased significantly after an unrewarded trial compared to a rewarded trial for both large positive errors and large negative errors.
source: In the same effector, variability increased significantly after an unrewarded trials compared to a rewarded trials (horizontal line, two-sample F-test for equal variances, ***p<<0.001) for both large positive errors (Monkey A: F(11169,10512) = 1.09, Monkey D: F(18540,13478) = 1.76) and large negative errors (Monkey A: F(8771,9944) = 1.40, Monkey D: F(21773,14889) = 1.62).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical tests comparing variability after rewarded versus unrewarded trials.

claim: The variability after an unrewarded trial of the same effector was significantly larger than after an unrewarded trial of the other effector.
source: The variability after an unrewarded trial of the same effector was significantly larger than after an unrewarded trial of the other effector (vertical line, two-sample F-test for equal variances, ***p<<0.001) for both large positive errors (Monkey A: F(11169,8670) = 1.20, Monkey D: F(18540,7969) = 1.32) and large negative errors (Monkey A: F(8771,5994) = 1.26, Monkey D: F(21773,7179) = 1.27).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical tests showing context-specificity of variability modulation.

claim: In humans, the variability was significantly larger after a negatively reinforced trial compared to a positively reinforced trial for both large positive errors and large negative errors.
source: In humans, the variability was also significantly larger after a negatively reinforced trial compared to a positively reinforced trial (horizontal line, two-sample F-test for equal variances, ***p<<0.001) for both large positive errors (F(5536,5805) = 1.19) and large negative errors (F(9366,9444) = 1.11).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical tests on human data showing reward-dependent variability modulation.

claim: In humans, the variability after a positively reinforced trial of the same effector was significantly lower than after a positively reinforced trial of the other effector.
source: The variability after a positively reinforced trial of the same effector was significantly lower than after a positively reinforced trial of the other effector (vertical line, two-sample F-test for equal variances, ***p<<0.001, F(14497,15250) = 1.10).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical tests on human data showing context-specificity.

claim: Across subjects and irrespective of the size of error, variability was significantly larger after incorrect compared to correct trials in the probabilistic reward experiment.
source: We compared behavioral variability after 'correct' and 'incorrect' trials separately for small (Figure 4D, left) and large (Figure 4D, right) errors. Across subjects and irrespective of the size of error, variability was significantly larger after incorrect compared to correct trials (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of the probabilistic reward experiment.

claim: In monkeys, σ0 and σSE but not σRS were significantly different between two effectors.
source: In monkeys, σ0 and σSE but not σRS were significantly different between two effectors (σ0: p<<0.001, one-tail two sample t-test, df = 482, t = 5.26; σSE: p<<0.001, two sample t-test, df = 482, t = 5.06; σRS: p=0.13, t-test, df = 261, t = 1.5 for the Short interval, and p=0.26, t-test, dt = 219, t = 1.1 for the Long interval).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of RSGP model parameters between effectors.

claim: In human subjects, variance terms were not significantly different between effectors.
source: In the human subjects, variance terms were not significantly different between effectors (p=0.03 for σ0, p=0.01 for σSE, and p=0.027 for σRS, two sample t-test, df = 118).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of RSGP model parameters between effectors in humans.

claim: The inactivation of thalamus has a much stronger effect on modulating animals' motor timing variability compared to DMFC and caudate.
source: For example, it has been shown that the inactivation of thalamus has a much stronger effect on modulating animals' motor timing variability compared to DMFC and caudate (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work showing differential effects of inactivation across brain areas.

claim: DMFC neurons have highly heterogeneous response profiles that evolve at different speeds depending on the interval.
source: Moreover, the nature of signals in DMFC-projecting thalamus and DMFC during motor timing are different: DMFC neurons have highly heterogeneous response profiles that evolve at different speeds depending on the interval, whereas thalamic neurons carr signals whose strength (i.e. average firing rate) encode the underlying speed.
evidence: The manuscript describes differences in neural coding between brain areas based on previous work.

claim: Thalamic neurons carry signals whose strength (i.e. average firing rate) encode the underlying speed.
source: Moreover, the nature of signals in DMFC-projecting thalamus and DMFC during motor timing are different: DMFC neurons have highly heterogeneous response profiles that evolve at different speeds depending on the interval, whereas thalamic neurons carr signals whose strength (i.e. average firing rate) encode the underlying speed.
evidence: The manuscript describes neural coding properties in thalamus based on previous work.

claim: In the thalamus, the reward adjusted the variance of average firing rates, but not the variance of speed.
source: As predicted by our hypothesis, the effect of reward on neural activity in the thalamus was different from that in the DMFC and caudate. In thalamus, the reward adjusted the variance of average firing rates, but not the variance of speed .
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of neural trajectory speed showing differential effects of reward across brain areas.

claim: In the DMFC and caudate, the reward modulated the variance of the speed at which neural trajectories evolve.
source: In contrast, in the DMFC and caudate, the reward modulated the variance of the speed at which neural trajectories evolve.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of neural trajectory speed showing differential effects of reward across brain areas.

claim: The reward-dependent modulation of neural trajectory speed was present only for consecutive trials associated with the same effector.
source: Moreover, these effects were present only for consecutive trials associated with the same effector.
evidence: The manuscript reports context-specificity of reward effects on neural trajectory speed.

claim: The region of thalamus recorded from receives information from three major sources: the frontal cortex, the output nuclei of the basal ganglia, and the deep nuclei of the cerebellum.
source: While we do not know which areas might directly control motor timing variability, we note that the area of thalamus we have recorded from receives information from three major sources, the frontal cortex, the output nuclei of the basal ganglia, and the deep nuclei of the cerebellum (Middleton and Strick, 2000; Kunimatsu et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on thalamic connectivity.

claim: Modulation of variability prior to movement initiation has been reported in motor and premotor areas.
source: Modulation of variability prior to movement initiation has been reported in motor and premotor areas (Churchland et al., 2006; Churchland et al., 2010), and distinct correlates of explore-exploit strategy have been found across multiple nodes of the frontal cortex (Hayden et al., 2011; Tervo et al., 2014; Ebitz et al., 2018; Massi et al., 2018; Sarafyazd and Jazayeri, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on variability modulation in cortical areas.

claim: The cerebellum plays a central role in trial-by-trial calibration of motor variables including movement initiation time.
source: Finally, the cerebellum plays a central role in trial-by-trial calibration of motor variables (Ito, 2002; Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Herzfeld et al., 2015) including movement initiation time (Ashmore and Sommer, 2013; Kunimatsu et al., 2018; Narain et al., 2018) and thus is a natural candidate for calibrating firing rates in thalamus, although how such calibration could be made reward-sensitive remains an open question (Hoshi et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on cerebellar function in motor calibration.
